utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning everybody. Good morning, Registrar. Can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are present. Prosecution is represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Absent amongst the Defence teams I notice Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Haynes. Is Mr. Nikolic here or not, because I can't see from here. No. And Ms. Nikolic. Okay. Good morning to you, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll continue with your testimony today. I don't think we'll finish today with you, but we'll try. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on Friday we were talking about smuggling of forbidden goods in convoys. Have you ever asked your subordinated units, including the intelligence organs, to analyse the activities of UNPROFOR? I am talking about the intelligence organs of Visegrad TG.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I asked the security organs and the intelligence organs to conduct an analysis of the flow and examination of convoys, the transport, and everything done when -- everything found when those convoys were examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D799. It's an intelligence and security report coming from the 1st Podrinje Brigade, addressed to the Drina Corps and to the Visegrad Tactical Group on the 4th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the first paragraph of this report. At the first paragraph of this report, mention is made of intelligence activities by humanitarian organisations. Do you recollect such activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, not only on the basis of this particular report, but also on the basis of many regular reports that were coming in to us. For the most part, the contents of those reports relate to the increased number of people in the convoys that were announced. And although these convoys did have permission not to be mixed, but in every convoys there were members of other organisations; that is to say, not those that had been announced beforehand. And mostly there were cases in which we found and seized technical resources which were not permitted. It was not permitted to bring them in to protected areas and in the area that UNPROFOR moved around.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Last Friday you told us that there were checkpoints in the Visegrad TG area of responsibility. Did you receive a specific information about the organisation of these checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... issue specific orders for commissions which were working at those checkpoints and specifically the activities that they were engaged in at those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D1267. It's an order from the Visegrad TG from 1993, but we can't read the date. It's illegible. Could we scroll down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here you see your name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English that's on the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The only thing I am interested here is to know whether this is an order related to the organisation of checkpoints, an order coming from you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, this is one of those orders, and on the basis of every order that I received from my superior command, I, in turn, issued my own orders to my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did incidents happen on the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not often, but they did happen, there were serious incidents from time to time when the inspections were being carried out of the convoys that were entering our zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D830. This is a report from the Podrinje Brigade, dated 8th of May 1993. Before the exhibit is displayed, I was wondering whether when there were incidents you were informed or notified of the fact personally by people who were at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: After every inspection I would receive oral reports, and within the frameworks of the regular daily combat reports, there was detailed description or reporting on how these inspections were conducted and how the control of the convoys was put in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of the page here, on page 1 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this refresh your memory? Do you remember this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well. I remember this report and the incident. It was a checkpoint at Rogatica, and this particular convoy was held back for three days; the reason being, that in the declaration for the passage of the convoy on the basis of the documents and what was found when the inspections were conducted, there were a series of irregularities that were found and they led to the incident, rather this, the fact that the convoy was blocked at the checkpoint, stopped from passing. Now, since the convoy was held at the checkpoint for three days, from the Main Staff, the people there intervened, specifically General Tolimir called me up personally and asked me to go to the spot and to see what was going on. That's what I did, I went to the site and found for myself that the commission which had examined and inspected the convoys worked in the proper manner, was consistent in its conduct without any ill-intent, and purposely keeping the convoy back for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that you remember this convoy because it was held back for three days. Do you remember another convoy that ran into difficulties as well in the same period of that particular year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that other convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D831. 5D831. A documented dated 9th of May 1994, the day after the incident we mentioned earlier. I don't want to spend too much time dealing with this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But I would likely to know the following: We are faced here with a situation where two incidents occur over two days. At the time you were the commander of the Visegrad TG. Did you ever receive any type of explanation from UNPROFOR about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Although, at that time, I was at the forward command post in Gorazde, or, rather, Kopaci, and although I had meetings daily with the commander of UNPROFOR -- or, rather, with the representatives of the UNPROFOR command in Gorazde, there was never an explanation as to why things like that were happening when the convoys were passing through.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any promise that this type of incident would never happen again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they would say it would not repeat itself, it would not happen again, but nonetheless there were always problems when the inspections were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when it was difficult for convoys to go through because of some restrictions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly they were periods when relations between the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the command of UNPROFOR were tense, then that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D827. This is a report from the Main Staff dated 11th of April, 1994. I'd like to have page 5 in English and page 4 in B/C/S on the screen, please. Page 5 in English. Could we zoom in on the last paragraph of page 4 in B/C/S for the witness to be able to read the text properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember this situation where the relations between the Main Staff and UNPROFOR had been suspended and when there were no more convoys?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, because we did receive orders from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that in April 1994 relations were difficult, do you remember why it was so? Do you remember why in April 1994 relations were tense?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not, specifically, but I assume that they were tense relations because of the threats of bombing and that they would open fire on positions of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could page 1 of the report be shown to the witness, please. In English that's page 2. Paragraph 1 -- first paragraph on page 2 in English and last paragraph on page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've saw that. Precisely because of the bombing and NATO opening fire from the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just so make sure that we understand each other, is there a connection between this paragraph and the fact that relations with UNPROFOR were suspended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember how long it lasted, how long relations were suspended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long, just a few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D828. This is a report from the Main Staff dated 14th of April, 1994, four days after the report we've just seen. Could the witness be shown page 3 both in English ask in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the last paragraph. Apparently four days later relations were still suspended, but there is one thing I am interested here. In this paragraph we can read that this was a decision of the Supreme Command. At the time when you were commander of the Visegrad TG, or even later when you were working at the Main Staff, did you know what was the influence of the Supreme Command and President Karadzic on decisions taken by the army of Republika Srpska with respect to convoys?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was not able to make decisions independently, to cut off contact with UNPROFOR. A decision of that kind was exclusively within the purview of the president of the republic, or, rather, the Supreme Command. He was the only person who was able to take that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Last Friday I put questions to you about Directive Number 5, and you stated that you had not seen the directive, but that you had received the order -- or an order related to that directive from your higher command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D1028.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this order connected to Directive Number 5?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order was addressed to the Visegrad TG, we can see that on -- at point or item 2, but I'm interested in item 3 where mention is made of the prevention -- of preventing the junction of enemy forces, and it's related to the Bihac and Bratunac Brigades. You received that order, so were you aware of what this meant at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time on the basis of this order, I knew that it was a question of preventing communication between the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Zeleni Jadar checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I arrived at the Main Staff, I heard that there were very big problems along the communication line of Zeleni Jadar-Skelani-Podravci [phoen]. When the protection zones were set up, that road, that communication line was under the command of the army of Republika Srpska. However, the forces of UNPROFOR from Srebrenica, most probably under pressure from the Muslim units, moved their checkpoints from the north, Srebrenica, towards Zeleni Jadar, in -- so that in the second half of 1994, that communication line was completely cut off. I personally was present with the -- with vice-president Koljevic, the late Koljevic, and a representative of the UNPROFOR command from Sarajevo, and the commander of the UNPROFOR forces from Srebrenica, along that communication line. And that was sometime in October 1994. When Commander Koljevic launched a protest because of UNPROFOR's conduct, and it was demanded that that checkpoint be returned to its initial position. The representative of the UNPROFOR command, Colonel Lemje [phoen], I remembered his name, he introduced himself, and said he was standing in for Victor Andreev, he accepted what the Serb side put to him. And he saw on the spot that the situation was as it was described, and he said that nothing could be done on the ground at that point in time but that he would refer back to the command and our requests and he hoped that the situation would be resolved. To the best of my knowledge that checkpoint was never moved, it was never moved back to the initial position so that the communication line between Zepa and Srebrenica remained open.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic now. When you were serving as Visegrad TG commander, did you receive any reports from your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were there any difficulties in the way these reports were transmitted and in the contents of these reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasional problems. There were situations in which reports did not arrive on time, they would be sent late, and some events or situations that had occurred in the zone would be first communicated to the superior command. There were no -- there were not many such situations, but they did occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to move on to 5D1263. I'd like to look at item 3. On the English version it starts on page 2 and runs into page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am familiar with this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This report refers to two potential causes of difficulties. Let's look at the technical difficulties. Did you have such problems, did you experience such problems on a regular basis or was this just a one-off?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not an isolated case. It did not happen often, however, it did happen from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you have any instance of the reports being erroneous?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show Exhibit 5D1013. This is a document from the General Staff, dated 26th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Apparently the assessment produced by the Drina Corps was erroneous. When you received similar reports or assessments, what could you do to assess the situation on the ground, specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I received an erroneous report from my subordinate command, I personally or my deputy would intervene. Since my area of responsibility was not large, we could follow and monitor the situation regularly, and we were familiar with the overall situation in our subordinate units. We would warn the commanders of the brigades not to send such reports, because we were familiar with the situation in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were there any instances when the reports were intentionally biased so as to improve the situation or give a different shine to the situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This didn't happen often, but it did happen, however. The commanders of subordinate units would touch up the situation at certain points in time, or would try to find a scapegoat if they did not carry out an order. They would not take the blame themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit 5D1014. It is a document stemming from the Drina Corps after --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: -- you had left Visegrad TG, dated 3 November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show item 11 to the witness. It's on page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a reflection of what I have just spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said your area of responsibility was not very large, but how could the commander of the corps, whose territory of area of responsibility was much larger, realise that these reports were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compared the reports of all the commands, you could conclude -- or, rather, he could conclude that reports were relative to the parts of the territories with the areas overlapped, and since the units also cooperated, it was obvious that the reports were controversial or did not reflect the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were serving at the Main Staff, did you have any opportunities to draft reports that were being sent back to the president?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you drafted these reports on the basis of the reports you had received, what did you feel and how did you assess the reports that the corps sent back to Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to rely on their reports if we did not have anybody from the Main Staff on the ground; however, we were experienced and our experience was valuable, so we could make our own -- own judgment based on every report whether it was just a formal report or whether it reflected the real situation. Erroneous or -- reports or parts thereof, would soon be discovered, they would be discovered already on the following day. If there was a cover-up on the following day, the truth would come to the fore. The report would be corrected by themselves in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where were you at the end of 1994, the beginning of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Krajina in the western part of the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when did you go to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was there anyone else from the Main Staff who went to Krajina with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic; the chief of the administration for airforce, General Jovo Maric; and after a month, we were joined by Colonel Ljubo Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you stay in Krajina until?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained there up until the second half of March during that stint. It was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did General Milovanovic stay until?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, General Milovanovic and the others returned towards the end of January or during the first half of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you came back from Krajina in March 1995, what duties did you perform at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from the forward command post, from Krajina, for a short period of time I remained at the Main Staff performing my regular duties as the chief of artillery in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then what mission did you receive, what brief did you receive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at the Main Staff during that period of time, I performed some analysis, the analysis of equipment and combat sets of artillery ammunition, since I was the chief of artillery. And I also performed some other tasks and duties relative to the tasks of the staff. Since the staff was not up to its full capacity, there are a lot of officers missing, there was a redistribution in place to allow for all the tasks to be performed in a quality and timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How long did you stay more in Crna Rijeka in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an order from General Milovanovic, and I went to the forward command post in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, before we move on to that period of time, I wanted to ask you the following question: Before you left for Zvornik, did you know of Directive Number 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an occasion to read the entire directive, but I learned about some provisions of that directive relative to some tasks that the military was supposed to carry out in the course of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit P5. It will be on page 2 of the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see here that the directive is dated 8 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 1 on English and page 3 in B/C/S. Could we maybe zoom in on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is the cover letter accompanying the directive when it was sent to the Drina Corps. It is dated 17th of March, 1995. What -- how were these documents and directives normally sent to subordinate organs and units? My question was not how was it transmitted but how fast, in what sort of timeline?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common practice for a directive or any other document of major importance to be signed by a superior officer, and then somebody from a subordinate command would be called immediately to take the document over and sign for it. I am talking about documents which bear the mark of secrecy or the mark of a state secret. If a document was confidential or strictly confidential, it could be dispatched by courier mail or by a courier. But, an accompanying letter would have to be signed to confirm the date and the time of the receipt of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to tell us about the fact that this letter was sent ten days after the directive was signed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and I'm sure I'm right, that this was too big a delay for a document which was strictly confidential and very important for further combat activities of the army of Republika Srpska, to be kept somewhere for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke about secret or state secrets. When a document bore the mention "state secret," did those people who hadn't worked directly on this document have any knowledge of the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafting of such documents involved their signing by all those who drafted it. Obviously, they were bound by a confidentiality clause, they had to keep the contents of such documents to themselves. Nobody else could be informed about the contents of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Final question on this document. Do you recognise the signature, just underneath the mention Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Milovanovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us that you spent a few months in Krajina alongside General Milovanovic. From your own experience and from what you know of the way General Milovanovic worked, was it possible that he could sign a document accompanying the directive without having read the directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier that you then went to Zvornik. Could you tell us more about what you were doing in Zvornik and what the operation was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Zvornik again with General Milovanovic, and I believe that General Jovo Maric was with us on that first day. Our objective was to go there and stay there for a month or so in the area of the Drina Corps and in the area of the East Bosnian Corps. Upon the order of the Main Staff, these two corps were preparing and carrying out an operation to liberate one part of the territory south of the Drina river. To be more specific, the area from Zvornik to -- towards Kalesija, Tuzla, Mount Majevica, all the way up to Brcko. As far as I can remember, this was Operation Spreca 95, an operation of operative significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to move on to 5D972.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke of an order from the Main Staff on the basis of which the corps prepared Operation Spreca. Do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this the order on the basis of which the corps prepared Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, after this order, did Main Staff -- or, rather, did the administration of operations and training within the Main Staff, have a role in preparing and planning for Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this order? No, it did not have any other tasks during the preparation and the carrying out of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the administration for operations and training of the Main Staff usually take part in the planning and preparing of operations at an operational level?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from an organisational order that was sent to the head and participants in the operation, and possibly some other people if that was necessary, if other orders were necessary, it did not take part in immediate planning and preparing of the operations or in carrying the operations out, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what about tactical combat? What was the role of the administration for operations and training in the Main Staff in tactical combat operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood it correctly that you are talking about the tactical level, that's the level of the brigade, then the Main Staff or the administration for operations and training had no assignments because it was a lower level, too low a level for the Main Staff to be included into such combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said General Milovanovic went to Zvornik with you. Was it usual for the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, to go on the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the field very often. And what I know from practice is this: We were together in Krajina for a longer period of time, then we were together again in Podrinje, or, rather, the area of the eastern Bosnia and Drina Corps, and then in Krajina once again. So my answer is very frequently. He was in the field often, sometimes for longer spells, sometimes for just a day or two or just one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was General Milovanovic's role during the spring of 1995 in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, pursuant to orders from the commander of the Main Staff, he had the role of setting up a forward command post. And from that forward command post, to follow developments and influence the course of operations. And before that, I know that General Milovanovic, first of all in the command of the Eastern Bosnian Corps, heard the decision and gave the okay and he would do the same in the command or at the forward command post, rather, of the Drina Corps, with the commander of the Drina Corps himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Right. Well, I'll come back to the way decisions were approved later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you 5D973. This is a report, or, rather, a letter from General Zivanovic. It was sent to the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS. This relates to Operation Spreca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But I'd like to look at this. When a letter is sent to the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, who is it actually addressed to? Can you tell us who the chief of the Main Staff is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that this kind of report was not customary, it wasn't usual to send out this kind of report. And that was because the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, to whom this letter is addressed, was present in the area of the Drina Corps and Eastern Bosnia Corps. And I personally think that a report written om this way had, as its objective, to leave a written trace for analysis or explanation after the operation had been carried out. And specifically, this letter or report was sent to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. Just for your information, we have a restructuring of the sitting schedule today. The first break will not be at 10.30 but at 10.20, and the break will be of only 20 minutes duration. Then we resume at 10.40, and we have a break at 12.00, which will be of 30 minutes. Last session, I will not be present, so we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Last session will resume at 12.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier orders that the Main Staff may have sent to corps relating to Operation Spreca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you 5D975. This relates to the 4th Serbian Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this the sort of order you thought -- you were thinking about when you said the Main Staff sent out orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you 5D976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps just to save some cross-examination time, if we could just have some clarification, because it's frankly just not clear to me from the witness' answer just now. When my friend refers to, in her question, "Were you thinking about when you said the Main Staff sent out orders," if we could just have some specificity as to exactly what the witness is talking about when he says "this is an example." Because we have been talking about a lot of Main Staff orders, and if we could just have some specificity on that issue, I think that would be more helpful for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's useful. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I think we can probably cover that question with the order I've just called up. They are very similar orders, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said, sir, that when an operation was being planned at an operational level, the planification was done by corps, and you said relating to Operation Spreca, that the Main Staff only sent out some specific individual orders. Now, is the order relating on the establishment of the 4th Brigade one such example of these specific orders that the Main Staff sent out to corps during Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. For operations at an operational level, it was the Main Staff who issues the basic order. In a specific case, it issued an order to establish the 4th Serbian Brigade. And another order that we see here linked to artillery support and rocket support to those engaged in this in carrying out the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness the second page of this document. The order has been initialed DM.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who -- or do you remember who drafted this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were when you drafted this order? Were you still serving in Crna Rijeka or were you already in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now come back to page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At item 2, your name appears. Could you tell us what is being referred to when planning tactical and technical preparation and the use of the aforementioned equipment is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, they were means and resources that not all the units had, and what they lacked especially were the technical resources used by -- well, for these bombs, air bombs. And for that reason, it was necessary to group the equipment so -- and have technical personnel inspect them, to see whether the crews were capable of carrying out their tasks, and that the organs planning the operation -- or, rather, the artillery plan of the operation, to check and see whether they were ready on the basis of the tactical and technical characteristics of the equipment and whether they could plan the targets and firing positions and the way in which this equipment was to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned air bombs. Were these weapons forbidden?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But I thought we had heard here that these weapons were not particularly accurate. Could you tell us anything about this and about the accuracy of such weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely for those reasons that it was necessary to plan things in detail to avoid having casualties on your own side, because the launchers, launchers which - how shall I say this? - were fairly primitively manufactured, had not been tested technically. They hadn't been tested ballistically. And so the way they were launched were not followed by necessary calculations, so these devices and this equipment was not precise. And very often there were very large deviations from one projectile to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn your attention to item 4, please. In item 4 we discuss the logistics sector, which was meant to receive instructions from the chief of operations and training administration. What was the chief of operations and training administration meant to be doing practically, according to this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew what this is about, because when I wrote the order I knew what I should focus on and what should be taken into account, that the transport of this equipment must be separate on different vehicles, motors on one vehicle, bombs on another vehicle. And since after I had written this order, I went into the field myself, I told the chief of operations about this order and gave him explanations and said that if the rear sector wanted explanations as to why so many vehicles were necessary and why that particular type of vehicle was necessary, that he could explain to them on my behalf, because I was no longer on the spot but I was in the field. So I explained to him the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you say you gave explanations. Would it be -- would it have been possible to send these orders individually without your instructions, without your information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is a mistake in English on 23, line 1. It wasn't "orders" but "information."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. It was your own question. Shall we have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. Next break at noon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, do you know where General Miletic or, rather, Colonel Miletic at the time, do you know where he was during Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that you've already mentioned the participation of the Drina Corps and of the Eastern Bosnia Corps in the Spreca operation. Do you know if anyone coordinated the operations of these two corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The coordination was conducted from the forward command post of the Main Staff in Zvornik. The coordination was conducted by General Milovanovic himself, together with -- or, rather, he was the commander of the forward command post, and I took part as well. General Jovo Maric would take part from time to time as well, and a number of other officers would spend a day or two at the forward command post coming from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was it possible to coordinate directly from Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not possible. Or, rather, it wouldn't have been effective, and that's why the forward command post was set up in the first place in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in the combat area as part of Operation Spreca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think until sometime in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D985.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And whilst the exhibit is being brought up, it's a report from the Drina Corps, I'd like to know whether you know until when General Milovanovic remained in that area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was not in the operation zone every day, but until mid-May, or the end of May he was there from time to time. He would go to the Eastern Bosnia Corps area and he would spend time at the Main Staff headquarters as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at item 2 of this report. It's a regular combat report from the Drina Corps dated 13th of May, 1995, and can you have a look at the last sentence of item 2 referring to the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that the chief of the Main Staff toured positions of the armoured detachment and 5th Infantry Battalion in the 1st Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When in a document of the VRS mention is made of the chief of the Main Staff, who is that person meant to be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on, you mentioned the fact that decisions needed to be approved. You were referring to decisions made by the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps and that were then approved by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D987. It's very difficult to decipher, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So to help you out, I am going to read out item 3 in English. [In English] "Execute the task under the Spreca 95 plan with available forces pursuant to the decision of the Drina Corps Commander which has been approved by me." [Interpretation] We can see the signature, typed signature, of General Milovanovic at the bottom of the page. Were you aware of a decision taken around the 20th of May 1995 and then approved by General Milovanovic, were you aware of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that decision was made earlier, before the start of the operation. Both corps commanders reported the decision and General Milovanovic approved it, and on the basis of those decisions the operation went forward. So it wasn't made on the 20th of May. It was the second half of March or the end of March, I am not quite sure which, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the Main Staff, who had the authority to approve decisions made by corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That exclusive right was vested in the commander of the Main Staff, or his deputy, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the head of administration for operations and training have that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't and nor did anybody else except the two men I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We mentioned the Muslim forces and what they were trying to achieve in 1994 and 1995 when you were at the Visegrad TG, they were trying to connect the enclaves, and I'd like to know the following: When you were in Zvornik, did you hear of movements by Muslim forces from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was mention of that during the evening analysis or reporting sessions, that the Muslim forces were expected to attack from the area of Srebrenica and Zepa with the aim of lifting the burden from their forces at Talocuk [phoen], or, rather, the area in which the Spreca operations were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D1213. This is an order coming from the Main Staff. It bears the signature, or, rather, the name of General Milovanovic. It is dated 30th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at the preamble of this order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If such a movement had taken place, could it have had an influence on Operation Spreca, on the way Operation Spreca unfolded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those forces were transferred, then that would be a great reinforcement to the forces at the front in the area in which Operation Spreca was being conducted. Now, whether it was those forces or reinforcements from the rear of the territory in-depth which was under control of the Muslims forces, during the operation itself, on several occasions there were strong counter-attacks launched by the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you came back from Zvornik, where did you go then? I mean, when you left Zvornik, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time relations with UNPROFOR were rather tense?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the bombing had started; that is to say, the shelling of the positions of Republika Srpska and the infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the end of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I went to Krajina again, together with General Milovanovic and General Jovo Maric.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you mention the Krajina, what do you mean exactly? Where exactly in Krajina did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the forward command post of the Main Staff in Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were the links between the Drvar forward command post and the main command post at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a direct protected link.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if General Milovanovic, whilst he was in Krajina, got in touch with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every evening the two of them spoke. General Milovanovic spoke to General Mladic every evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if General Milovanovic had contacts with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did have communication with General Miletic, who was still colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to draft a directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what directive it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where were you when you drafted it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This directive was drafted at the forward command post of the Main Staff in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why was this directive drafted at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because most of the Main Staff, or the inner Main Staff headed by commander General Mladic, was in Banja Luka at the time; i.e., they were at the forward command post in Banja Luka and in the western part of the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D999.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Directive Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain how this directive was drafted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This directive was drafted by the so-called short -- or shortened procedure, and the most appropriate explanation for this method is as follows: At a meeting that the commander of the Main Staff had with his assistant -- assistants, the Chief of Staff, and others whom he considered important and who he thought should be present at the meeting, a short analysis of a situation in a given area was carried out. In this specific case, a short analysis referred to the situation in the areas of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps. All organs, i.e., all assistants, put forth their positions and opinions, since during their working days they all were on the ground in one of the relevant units. Based on that analysis, a conclusion was reached that it was impossible to defend the territory in question of Republika Srpska by mounting defence only. It was necessary to launch a counter-offensive. General Mladic put forth the main idea. He issued his orders in a very short outline, and he ordered others to draft a directive. After the meeting ended, General Milovanovic called me into his office. He gave me very specific tasks, he gave me instructions as to how to draft the directive, and he ordered me to draft it. When the directive was drafted, I took it to General Milovanovic, he read it, and then he took it to the commander of the Main Staff for signing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you page 4 in English and 3 in B/C/S. And could we scroll down the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see that this relates to the Sarajevo Corps, to the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to the following page B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Herzegovina Corps and the Drina Corps. Do you remember who told you what you were supposed to include in these sections of the directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In just the shortest outlines, the main tasks were distributed by General Mladic, and then General Milovanovic provided further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the very last page of this directive, page 5 in English and it's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Under item 7, mention is made of Directive Number 7. Who --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it's the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who told you that you should mention Directive Number 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not participate in the drafting of Directive Number 7 and since there were no other professional organs who could provide detailed elements for this particular point, he just -- General Milovanovic said that we should follow the spirit of Directive Number 7 when we wrote about the support to combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to the very last page of the document in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can see here at the bottom of the page that this directive was compiled by Colonel Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I would like to state that the -- the word "izrodio" is the word used in both texts in B/C/S, but in English a different translation has been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you attended the meeting prior to the drafting of the directive, what was your task during that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made notes during the analysis of the situation. I did not participate in the analysis myself. I did not intervene, I did not provide any contributions, I just made notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you -- or were you able to exert any type of influence on the content of the directive? You compiled this directive. As such, was your role the same as someone drafting the directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I drafted the directive based on the elements that I received at the meeting and later on from General Milovanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we move along too far, I tried to locate the word "izrodio" and just so the record is clear, can we have some clarification as to what's that's referring to. My friend made a -- a reference it was being used in both texts in the B/C/S, but there is a different translation. Can we just be told what that is so we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Thayer. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the word that comes just before Colonel Dragisa Masal, in English it's translated by "compiled," but in Directive Number 7 the exact same word is used in B/C/S but it was translated by "drafted" in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that's -- I think that's clear enough. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One point of clarification from me as well. I believe I am guilty. Here I spoke too fast --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Because your answer to one of my questions is not recorded on the transcript. So I am going to repeat that question to you. Do you have -- or were you able to exert an influence on the contents of a directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that the directive was drafted following the shortened procedure. What would your role have been if the usual and full procedure had been applied?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle the role of a person who drafts a directive does not differ that much. The only difference lies in the fact that when it comes to the complete method, all the organs of the Main Staff draft their own contributions for the directive, and they submit their contributions to the person who compiles or drafts the final version of the directive. So the only difference between the full or complete method and shortened method lies in the fact that the drafter has to write everything, and when it comes to the complete method he actually receives already written parts of the directive that he then merges. To put it simply, the drafter of a directive has a much easier time if the method is complete or full rather than shortened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When Directive Number 9 was compiled and brought to General Mladic, do you remember whether he signed it as it was or whether he corrected part -- or modified part of the directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not sign the directive immediately. He had some corrections to make. After that, General Milovanovic returned the directive to me, I changed it accordingly, and then the directive was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you include General Mladic's amendments in the final text of the directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had to. I didn't have a choice, did I?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did General Miletic take any part in the drafting of Directive 9?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that in those days almost all of the commanders of the Main Staff were located in Eastern Bosnia -- in Western Bosnia. Did you have -- did you know if the commanders had any meetings with his assistants in those days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost every day. Not every day but whenever the situation so allowed, when the assistants returned from the ground in a normal time, then in the evening they would analyse the situation of the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the commanders -- the commander and his assistants were in Western Bosnia, where were the Main Staff's decisions taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. The commander and his assistants were there, i.e., most of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did General Mladic consult General Miletic in making his decisions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Miletic was not in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where General Miletic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic was in Crna Rijeka at the Main Staff there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know what he did in Crna Rijeka in those days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since some of the officers were at the Main Staff, others were in the areas of other corps. General Miletic was there to receive reports, reports coming from the areas of all subordinate commands. He was supposed to merge these reports and send them to the Supreme Command. His task was also to organise the work with the remainder of the Main Staff that was in Crna Rijeka to look after the communications, and the work of the signals unit that was in charge of the communication with the Main Staff, that unit was in Crna Rijeka; and his task was also to possibly convey orders that he received from the commander to the other units of the army of Republika Srpska; for example, to the Herzegovina Drina, and Sarajevo Romania corps. This would be the task that Colonel Miletic performed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show page 1 of this directive to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The directive is dated 28th of September, 1995. Do you know when the directive was sent out to the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same evening when it was drafted, or, rather, when it was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to show you 5D1347. It is Directive Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who drafted this directive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know from what you can read where the directive was drafted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The directive was drafted at the forward command post in Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who was your superior officer in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, we have seen that General Milovanovic spent most of his time that year outside Crna Rijeka, some time in Zvornik, and a lot in Krajina. Who was the head of the Main Staff while General Milovanovic was in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in Crna Rijeka and General Milovanovic was not, who was in a position to give you orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Milovanovic was not in a position to get in touch with me, I received my direct orders from the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a clarification. On page 35, line 4 of my transcript, the question was put: "Who was the head of the Main Staff while General Milovanovic was in Krajina?" The terminology sometimes in extremely important. I don't know whether that's translation issue or that was the question that was asked, but I don't know if it was supposed to be who was chief of the Main Staff or head, but I think that needs some clarification either way just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you get the gist of his problem -- of his concern? Okay. Then you can address it perhaps, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understand what my learned colleague is saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, I would like to put that question in English. [In English] Who was the chief of the Main Staff when General Milovanovic was in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've spoken about orders you got. Did General Miletic ever serve as your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. There was a period, though, when we considered informally a possibility for the chiefs of branches to be integrated into the operations for training and operations. We opposed that, i.e., the chiefs of all branches opposed that. So the chiefs of all the branches were still directly subordinate to the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, even after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was General Miletic an advisor to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not his advisor. Nobody in the Main Staff was General Mladic's advisor. Nobody was an advisor to the commander of the Main Staff. He only had his assistants by establishment, he did not have any advisors at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was General Miletic's position within the Main Staff such that he could advise General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not his duty to provide advice. In the staff, everybody had his own tasks, and within the purview of their competences, they may have issued proposals. And whether the commander of the Main Staff would accept those or not, it was his discretionary right. So he could not give him any advice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. One moment, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's your turn now, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Break will be at 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I represent General Gvero and I'll have some questions for you. In answering questions today, General, you said that you returned to the western part of Republika Srpska sometime towards the end of May 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason, why did you return? Were there any changes in the situation in that part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was passed by the commander of the Main Staff upon the proposal of the chief, General Milovanovic, and the main reason was the fact that the operative and tactical situation in the western front had become more complicated. Part of the territory that was in the hands of the army of Republika Srpska had been lost. We expected a major offensive to be launched by the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian army in the western part of the front, and that is why the team from the Main Staff was sent to the western part of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that offensive followed soon afterwards, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In that offensive, the Croatian and Muslim forces took control of the elevations in the surrounding parts so that our forces were under siege, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian army sometime until the end of June and beginning of July, took control of Dinara and came within the vicinity of Grahovo and was in the rear of Knin. On the other side, most of Golija mountain was taken control of by the Croatian army, and Glamoc was threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood your testimony so far, General, the forward command post of the Main Staff was in Jasenica, and after that a command post was established in Drvar, right? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. The forward command post in Jasenica was formed at the end of October 1994 and I stayed there until the second half of March, myself. And the forward command post in Drvar was set up immediately after the new year; that is to say, the beginning of January 1995, in Drvar. And it was operational until the end of January or beginning of February. And then afterwards it was reactivated at the end of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of July 1995, you, yourself, were at Jasenica, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part I spent every day at the forward command post, or, rather, in a part of the front that we called Gruposko Bihacko [as interpreted] front. The others were at the Grahovo-Glamoc area at the forward command post at Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, when Grahovo and Glamoc fell, did you go to that part of the battlefront?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when Grahovo fell, General Milovanovic called me to come to Drvar straight away. So that very same day I arrived in Drvar pursuant to an order from General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown exhibit P3905.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, may I just take a moment, please. It's a combat report describing the situation on the front. The date is the 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 4 of this document, please. May we have that put up on e-court, and on English it is on page 5. May we scroll down, please, and see the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, look at that last paragraph there, please, which begins with "In the area of responsibility of the 30th infantry division ..." In the second half of that it says: "In the southeastern part of the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, the broader region of Grahovo and Grahovo itself, the population left the area heading towards Drvar and then further on to Petrovac and Sanski Most due to the fierce shelling of Glamoc, from which people continued to move out." People continued to move out of the town. So is that the day that you arrived to see General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the 27th, then that is the day when, to all intents and purposes, Grahovo fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Milovanovic issue an assignment of any kind to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were moving, he informed me that Grahovo had fallen and that there were no links with the Glamoc anymore, that he didn't know what was going on, and he ordered me to get into a car and to use the Drvar-Glamoc road, Glamocko Polje road, at the village of Rore, to go to Glamoc that way, and to see what the situation was like and then to come back and report to him about what I had found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you carry out the assignment General Milovanovic gave you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the road to Glamoc, when passing through the Serbian villages along the way, I didn't see a soul. The population had already moved out, and before entering Glamoc itself, I heard explosions. I stopped in the airport area. It's the airport belonging to the former JNA, with a grass takeoff and landing strip. And on -- in one facility there were two or three persons in uniform there. They said that there was nobody left in Glamoc and that it wasn't a good idea for me to go further on. In view of the situation, and as I saw that there were no soldiers along the way or any civilians, I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you arrived at the command post where you met General Milovanovic, did you happen to see any of the officers from the Main Staff there on that same day, the 27th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of July, I know full well that when I arrived that in the office of General Milovanovic, General Jovo Maric was there. And you could see that he had been crying, and when I asked what had happened before I reported myself, he just said very briefly, I had to evacuate my old folk from Grahovo. Then I went on to report briefly and went to the operations room, so except for the officers that were there that evening, I don't remember seeing anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see General Gvero at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for General Gvero, I did see him at the forward command post. As far as I remember -- as far as I remember that was on the following day or that evening, I can't be quite sure of that, but I think it was the next day that General Gvero was present at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa -- Mr. Haynes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, so that we can continue with that theme, on the 27th of July of 1995, as you've told us, Grahovo fell with the result that the Serbian population was moved out of the town. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you haven't dealt with this. You're aware, aren't you, of the Croatian forces that were involved in the taking of Grahovo. Can you tell us a little bit about them and the calibre of those forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we had, the information we had through our intelligence and by intercepting conversations along the air waves, we concluded that Grahovo had been taken control of by elite Croatian units; specifically, Grahovo itself had been taken control of by the Guards Brigade from Split. I don't know what the number was of that brigade, but I know that it was the Guards Brigade from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the next objective of the Guards Brigade from Split was Drvar itself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that after the 27th of July a brigade known as the Drinski Brigade was ordered to be put together under the command of my client general -- now General Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This axis, Grahovo-Drvar, was closed off by the Drina Brigade. I don't know what day it was brought in, but I do know that it stopped a further breakthrough from Grahovo towards Drvar. Somewhere around the village of Resanovci, that level, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were aware, weren't you, that that brigade had to be put together at very short notice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, it was put together in a brief period of time and was brought to the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if you would, what were your impressions of the military action carried out by that brigade under the command of then Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was in the area of combat operations, I know personally that the Drina Brigade managed to stop the further advance of the Croatian army. It was given the assignment of launching a counter-attack, and all the preparations were underway, and it was a classical example of artillery preparation which lasted 20 minutes to half an hour. And a fierce attack, they inflicted great casualties on the enemy. Now, in the Croatian information media, or, rather, they published three days a morning in Split, three days a morning in Split were proclaimed by the media, and I think that that day about 60 combatants from the Guards Brigade from Split were killed. Unfortunately, because the other units failed to function effectively, the ultimate goal was not achieved; that is to say, to take control of Grahovo again. So if you don't use the opportunity afforded you, then many problems ensue and indeed this brigade had many problems later on. The.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In summary then, would you say it was a classically executed military operation by a commander with a force he had put together at very short notice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it was a school example, a classic example of rapid planning and rapid deployment, rapid putting an operation into effect by a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was your observation of that consistent with your impression throughout your knowledge of him -- of Vinko Pandurevic as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. He had the skill to size up the situation, carry out preparations, and go into action, in keeping with the situation on the ground. So he acted energetically, which was this unit's general characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it may seem a little illogical but I'm going to go back in time, please to 1993. You told us that on the 4th of February of 1993, you became the commander of the tactical group at Visegrad. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your immediate predecessor in that role was Vinko Pandurevic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the military situation that you found yourself in when you first arrived in Visegrad was very difficult. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Muslims forces were on the surrounding hills above the town, they were able to shell it at will, and they had military ambition to take further territory in the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, during 1993 - and you've already spoken about this - there were two military operations, both called Mac, Mac 1 and Mac 2 in May and June of 1993. You've told us about them. I imagine you recall them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
