utterances.text: I don't know what operation you meant. You said "sibice." It was Mac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I perhaps should have said -- used the English word so it was translated to you, the word in English is "sword", translated into Serbian, that's Mac. So there was Sword 1 and Sword 2, to you Mac 1 and Mac 2. Sorry for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the tactical group employed to carry out those operations was comprised of a number of battle groups, and battle groups 1 and 2 were commanded by Vinko Pandurevic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, combat groups 1 and 2 were under the command of Vinko Pandurevic, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you're aware that at that time he had been taken from his position as commander of the Zvornik Brigade to command those battle groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brief explanation. He was not transferred from his own duties to take over these combat groups. He was there -- he brought in part of his unit as reinforcement to the zone of operations. And from part of the Visegrad tactical group and his unit, went to form two combat groups of which Vinko Pandurevic was directly in command and I think he was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. In those circumstances according to your understanding of the rules of the army of Republika Srpska, who would have been in command of the Zvornik Brigade while he was away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he was outside his own area, the area of his brigade, he was supposed to be replaced by his Chief of Staff when he was absent, if he had one, I assume he did have a Chief of Staff, so if he was absent that would be the person. So if the brigade was away in its original area, then it's the Chief of Staff that's in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is there, in your view, any need for any order from corps command to appoint the Chief of Staff as commander of the brigade in those circumstances, or does it follow automatically from the rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, command and control principles, if the brigade commander had a Chief of Staff who was at the same time the deputy commander, then there was no need to write out a separate order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on to a particular aspect of the operations we were talking about, Sword 1 and Sword 2. One of the towns or villages you've mentioned as being relevant to those actions was the town of Ustipraca. Do you remember that place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a settlement, a suburb of Gorazde in fact. I'd call it a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was the commander of the Muslim units in Ustipraca somebody called Ammo Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you mean Ammet Sejdic. He was the commander of the Muslim Visegrad brigade. And during the operation, he spent time in the village of Mejedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the operation, did a civilian population at Ustipraca become, as it were, trapped and isolated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As our forces, specifically the 1st and 2nd combat group, had cut off the communication line in Ustipraca, then the entire civilian population from Visegrad to Ustipraca - and this was a stretch of some 15 kilometres - they were cut off in the canyon, and both the Muslim army and the civilian population. And I would say there were between 2 and 3.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the evening, I received a report from my interception service that they had intercepted an attempt at contact between Ammet Sejdic, the commander of the Muslim forces, who was persistently calling Vinko Pandurevic up. And I was told by the people manning the interception devices, was that he was asking Pandurevic to enable the civilian population to pull out. Pandurevic answered and said that he guaranteed that the civilian population would not be targeted and that they had the night at their disposal to evacuate towards Gorazde. During the following day when we entered the territory which was under the control of the Muslims forces, we did not come across a single civilian. Not dead, not alive, nobody. We came across no soldiers, either. Now, whether the soldiers had fled before the civilians or after the civilians had left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that sort of behaviour negotiating with the enemy over the safety of civilians consistent with your impression of Vinko Pandurevic and his attitudes particularly to civilians during the course of this war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His conduct did not surprise me. He was a professional, and I personally think that the vast majority of army professionals would have acted in similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to finish before the break with you, General Masal, but what were your impressions of him in terms of his moral standards in the way he behaved as an army officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I had ample opportunity to cooperate and work together with Pandurevic in battle and then and later on I had a very high opinion of Pandurevic as a professional soldier. And I think he was a young officer, to be brief, who in the most effective way possible put the knowledge he had gained in his military schools into practice very well during the war. He had very high capabilities in the field of control and command of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, General Masal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. You'll start your cross-examination, Mr. Thayer, after the break. The break now will be of 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you were informed, Judge Agius will not be with us due to official business until Wednesday, so, therefore, we will be sitting pursuant to 15 bis. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. My name is Nelson Thayer, I will be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A couple of odds and ends first, General, based on some of the things you testified about this morning. You were shown an exhibit and there was a code name that was referred to in the exhibit. I can show it to you if you -- if you need to look at it to refresh your recollection, but you were asked some questions about, I think on that occasion, you said that it was a little difficult to get in contact with the party that you wanted to be in touch with. And the document referred to the code name "Diploma." Do you recall what that code name referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that code name was for the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately what period of time the Main Staff used that code name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think that it was used up to sometime in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 5D1026, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to show you, General, a document you were shown two copies of yesterday, it was the same thing only one of them, I think, actually bore General Mladic's signature. You identified both. I just want to ask you about one paragraph in it. Do you see paragraph 3 in your language, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you confirm for the Trial Chamber that at the time you received this order, you were familiar with the Geneva Conventions, their protocols 1 and 2, the 1907 Hague convention on the laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with the Geneva Conventions. I learned about them during my education and also from the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia. We had to be aware of certain provisions of the Geneva Conventions, maybe, not of the entire document but of certain provisions, certain ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I understand from what you're telling us that some of your training occurred during your professional JNA training, and then there was additional training during the period where you were serving in the VRS as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe what kind of training was undertaken throughout the VRS during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not classical training. All the commands and all the units at all levels had to be informed and knew about certain provisions of the Geneva Conventions that dealt with prisoners of war, treatment of civilians, treatment of various types of infrastructure in the territory that is used for the survival or, rather, life of the civilian population on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, General, just so you know, if I'm looking away from time to time or not engaging with you, it's simply I'm trying to either look at the transcript that I have here running based on our question and answer, and I'm also waiting for the translation to complete. I want to ask you a couple of questions about the Spreca operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could 5D982, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you testified about Operation Spreca, as we all know. I don't know if you had had an opportunity to look at this particular document during your proofing. It I don't believe was used by my learned friend for the Miletic team during her examination, but it was on the exhibit list. So if you need some time to take a look at the document, please do so. If you recognise it and you are familiar with its contents, please say so and I will get right to my questions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. And I know that this analysis was carried out at the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this analysis was carried out after this operation had been underway for approximately a month; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Without going into the specifics, it's fair to say that the operation was encountering some difficulties which required this analysis to be conducted and which further required the presence and involvement of some Main Staff officers to provide their insight and guidance during this process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Getting right to the point, General, the situation was a serious one at this time and there was a lot at stake; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was serious. I don't know what you mean when you say that there was a lot at stake. I know what the situation was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The colonels -- the Main Staff colonels Pandzic and Djurdjevic were there and made an assessment and provided briefings on behalf of the Main Staff after which certain conclusions were made. Do you recall that, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pandzic and Colonel Djordjevic were present when the analysis was taking place, and their objective was to look at all of the data and information or, rather, what the command of the Drina Corps was doing in order that Spreca 95 should be carried out as was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 5D2891, please. Actually, that's 5DP02891. I think that will work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, General, just take a look the document. If you need some time to scan through it, please do so. It's just two pages, so take your time, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And may we see page 2 in B/C/S and English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you've already testified about being present at this Main Staff forward command post. I think you identified General Milovanovic, General Maric, yourself and other Main Staff officers who would come and go during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, General Maric, not Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, that was my pronunciation, General. Now, on the first page of this document we saw that yourself was identified as well as Colonel Trkulja, do you remember whether Colonel Trkulja was present at that IKM, that Main Staff IKM during this period of time as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Colonel Trkulja was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that this is a very serious senior group of Main Staff officers who are assigned to this IKM?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the second page of this order - and I want to direct your attention, General, to paragraph 7 - it says that: "The commands of the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps will allocate one operative each and one assistant commander for morale, religious and psychological preparation if the corps who will be a part of the force of the IKM of the Main Staff in Zvornik..." Do you see that, General, paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were at this IKM. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why General Mladic deemed it important in this order to have a corps level assistant commander for morale actually present in the Main Staff forward command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of an analysis conducted by the command of the Drina Corps, they arrived at the conclusion that the rate of the operations, Operation Spreca, rather, was on the decline, that the tempo was on the decline, and the main problem was coordinating the units, the action of the units taking part in the operation. And after the operation had been in force for one month, there was a lag, a lull, due to casualties suffered and the fact that the set goals had not been reached. So in part morale was low among the fighters. And that certainly prompted the commander of the Main Staff to issue the order that, at the forward command post, organs for operative affairs be included and organs for morale and other legal issues be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to be fair to the witness, when my colleague stated who was identified to go to the forward command post, he should give the opportunity to the witness to tell us who was the leader of that team, because another person is mentioned, not by name but by his function. So if this could be clarified, maybe. I am talking about item 1 on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can -- I think I can clarify, but I think my first "general" out of my mouth was the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and I believe that's to whom my friend is referring. But for the sake of the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's it. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall, General, what the corps level assistant commander for morale was doing during this period of time to help, I presume, and correct me if I'm wrong, make sure that the combat morale was at the appropriate level and correcting whatever the insufficiencies were in the level of morale that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Just a second. I see Mr. Josse is on his feet. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be worth the witness taking off his earphones, assuming he doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Masal, do you understand English? I haven't heard your answer, whether you speak and understand English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you take off your headphones, please. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position here is that these questions are being asked frankly rather out of the blue to this particular witness, by my learned friend. They were certainly not issues that we touched upon in the course of our cross-examination at all. So far as morale is concerned, they weren't issues that my learned friend for General Miletic touched upon during her examination in chief of the witness. Of course, the rules do allow a party to ask questions that are relevant to their case, and that is presumably what Mr. Thayer is doing here, but we just want to flag up that we are completely defenceless in this situation, totally and utterly. Witnesses are called, beyond our control, by another party to the case, we don't know whether to ask some questions, any questions, no questions. We have no idea what the Prosecutor is going to ask, we don't know in advance what their list of -- what their list of documents are, and even if we did, it wouldn't help very much. And frankly, we are completely helpless in this situation. We have discussed this amongst ourselves over the last few days and have decided that if it happened again to flag it up to the Trial Chamber. We allowed my learned friend to ask one question, he asked that question, he's now being persistent in asking another question. Realistically, as I've already said, the rules allow him to do this. And I just want to emphasize that this is grossly unfair, not on his part but in relation to the general procedure that's being adopted and that General Gvero is really helpless in the present given situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you be -- will your concerns be resolved if the Chamber is minded to consider whether to allow you a further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, certainly, that would allay our fears to some extent and would allow us to address these particular issues, but that would -- I mean, it's a matter I want to discuss specifically with Mr. Krgovic, but that would be an offer that we would accept, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I -- with all due respect to my friend, I think he's overstating his and his client's helplessness in this circumstance and all the other circumstances where we've had witnesses called by one party and then cross-examined by other Defence teams. What we have seen throughout the Defence case are witnesses from one Defence team being proofed by one or more other Defence teams. We can see from the questions that are being asked on what are purportedly cross-examinations, are clearly questions that have been prepared in advance with the aid of proofing sessions of these witnesses. There is nothing to prevent my friend, as he has done with other witnesses, clearly, based on the questions that were asked, meeting with any of these witnesses ahead of time - and I believe they have done so on numerous occasions - so I think this idea that they are helpless is absolutely unfounded. They see the documents that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's stop here. We have heard enough. And then we proceed. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider in due course whether to allow further cross-examination by the Gvero Defence, if necessary. That said, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, sorry for the little intermission. My question was: You were at this IKM. What did this corps level assistant commander for morale do during this period of time to rectify the deficiencies in morale that you told the Trial Chamber about a little while ago? What kind of measures were undertaken, what kind of actions did this assistant commander undertake?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what they did individually, because I spent most of the time in the field myself, but I assume that it would follow from this kind of order or from this order that they were -- what was necessary was to talk to the commanders, the commanders commanding the operation, and that most probably, according to their plan or pursuant to orders from their commanders, they would go into the units, the units that took part in carrying out this operation. I was not with them myself because I had my own assignments which I had to carry through, but from the order I assume that those were the tasks they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to different topic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me move on to a new topic. You've told us about the considerable amount of time you've spent at various IKMs on various fronts during 1995. I just want to ask you some questions about your duties and responsibilities as chief of artillery for the Main Staff. Can you just briefly describe what those were? And I'm talking separate and apart from whatever your duties were when you were forward during those periods of time you talked about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon taking over the duties of chief of artillery in the Main Staff, the main thing was for me to see and later to take into account and take care of artillery units who were in the army of Republika Srpska, to see to them. Now, according to the formations and the tactical units, the operative composition of the corps, and the strategy of the army as a whole, the artillery was grouped in such a way as to ensure that each unit had its own artillery which it was in command of directly. Now, the specific feature in the army of Republika Srpska was as follows: All the units at all levels, except for the Main Staff, had their own artillery units. We had a rocket brigade as well, which establishment-wise, should have been immediately subordinated to the commander; that is to say, that it would come under me as an establish unit. However, because of its location, the location of that unit, at the very beginning of the war it was attached to the 1st Krajina Corps so that as I did not have -- or, rather, the Main Staff did not have under its immediate command a single artillery unit, my basic task was to see that the artillery units were properly used in the units lower down and to take care and see and keep records of their technical equipment, the ammunition, artillery ammunition for those units, and to be in control of the artillery caters, the men, and to make proposals for promotions, training, and moving people around, that kind of thing. Since the scope of the duties of the chief of artillery had been made more narrow, because we didn't have these units immediately under our direct command, that is why I had to perform the other tasks at the forward command post as well and all over the front, in actual fact, where combat was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, when you that your "... basic task was to see that the artillery units were properly used in the units lower down," what are you were talking about there practically speaking? Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that actually means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms it would mean the following: When I toured the subordinate units and when I went into the field, I would look to see whether the artillery was grouped according to their purpose for deployment, or, which was often the case, the artillery was split and then assigned all over the front, which, in principle, is not how the artillery should be deployed during combat. So I would make a note of such cases and make proposals to the corps commanders instructing them how they should deal with the situation and also to report back to General Milovanovic, my superior officer, about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Presumably, on your part, General, that would require a fair amount of knowledge about the activities at a particular point in time within the corps so that you could make that assessment as to whether the artillery was being properly deployed and so forth; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should just like to add that after taking over these duties, some 15 to 20 days afterwards, I managed to tour all the corps and to size up the situation on the spot to see the state of the artillery and how it was grouped, and on the basis of that and later on during the operations where I was present, I was able to have an overview of the situation and see whether the artillery was used properly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions on this topic, General. Can you give us an idea - and let's start from the bottom up - when authorisation was required or not for artillery assets to be employed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the process of preparation for all combat activities at all levels, whether it be combat or fighting, at the level of a battalion, a brigade or an operation at the level of a corps, or the army as a whole for that matter, in the planning process, each and every commander has to plan how the artillery is to be deployed and its effects. If there is a professional under his command, then it is this professional officer who would be in charge of compiling such a plan which he signs when he completes the plan, but it is authorised by the commander just as the commander authorises the -- and makes the overall decision, the ultimate decision. So the deployment of the artillery -- in the deployment of the artillery each command is autonomous, every commander, it is the exclusive right of the commander to have right over the deployment of the artillery based on proposals from the chief as the professional organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And even with that autonomy that you just told us about, were there any circumstances under which a commander would require authorisation from his superior command in order to actually utilise his artillery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are situations when the commander, or, rather, the lower level commanders, can issue orders to use the artillery itself. And that is in the case of a surprise attack, for instance, when you have to refute such an enemy attack by all means available, and the command of the artillery unit, if he -- his positions have been directly attacked, then he, too, can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 5D976, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, this is going to be a document that you were shown just, I think, this morning. And I just had a couple of questions based on the questions that you were asked just this morning on it. Do you see the document and do you recognise it from your discussion this morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: These air bombs that you told us about, can you briefly describe how they actually were fired? I think you described a launching system and trailers and so forth, but can you just describe how they worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, you have a motor vehicle and the body of the vehicle in which you have incorporated part of a classical artillery piece known as the cradle. So all you have is the cradle without the barrels, and welded on to that is a rail similar to a tram rail or railway lines for trains. And that is the device used for launching. It has targeting devices from artillery pieces which was used for this cradle. Now, the aerial bomb itself, as a whole, remains as it is. In order to launch it or to expel it from this device, at the back it had a metal adapter built into it, a metal plate or adapter, with an incised device for the rocket motor, 1, 2, 3, or 4 of those. And these rocket motors were used with a multiple barrel rocket launcher; specifically, in this case, it was a multiple barrel of 122 millimetres of Russian manufacture called Grad, and on the underside there were two slips which led the bomb along the tracks or rails. And the third element was a device for electric activation, the activation of the motor itself, and this activation was done on the side, on the flank, from a distance of about 10 metres. Since the rocket motors, once they are activated, expel the flair or flame, the substance of the -- that is how those aerial bombs were launched using this particular device.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described the flame from the rocket. Is it correct then that there is some type of fuel that is powering these rockets? How did they actually get their power? Was it through some type of fuel source?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, and I don't think you understood me, that we used original rocket engines. This was taken from the multiple rocket launcher, and it is separate, and it contains fuel -- rocket fuel. This means that it was part of another device that we used, and that's what we used to fuel our VBR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll move on, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions, Mr. President, and I will tie this into something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this artillery?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I will tie this in to a specific document that is relevant to this case. Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony about aerosol bombs, General. What are aerosol bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not an aerosol bomb. It says here it's FAB, food [as interpreted], gas, air bomb which is a classical bomb filled by material of a certain weight, 100 kilos, or 275 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, General. My question is what is an aerosol bomb, what is the difference between the avio-bombe that you've just told us about and an aerosol bomb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a professional, but I only heard of aerosol projectiles. I've never had an occasion to meet with aerosol projectiles in my practice. An FAB is exclusively used to have impact power, destruction power, which is inflicted by iron particles, and this is the kind of shells that I know. I've only heard of aerosol bombs, but I've never had an occasion to see them in practice or attend such projectiles being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P03025.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, what you have on your screen before you is the combat order issued by Commander Blagojevic for the Krivaja 95 operation, the operation against the Srebrenica enclave. What I want to show you is page 4 of the B/C/S and that's also page 4 of the English, and it's at paragraph 6.2. And do you see where it says: "At 0300 hours on 6 July it will fire four projectiles," it's referring to the rocket launcher platoon "... it will fire four projectiles, 50 kilogram avio-bombe on the Potocari sector. My question for you, General, is what's listed here, these 50 kilogram avio-bombes, these were what you were talking about a few moments ago, not aerosol bombs but the air bombs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, you testified about being at the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka until some time around the end of May. I think your recollection was that the NATO air strikes had already happened before you left. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe a few days before we left for Krajina was when the first NATO air strike -- air strikes happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to make sure we are talking about the same events, these were the air strikes in 1995 when directly preceded the taking of the UNPROFOR hostages and the television images we all recall about some of the peacekeepers being placed at various installations. Are we on the same page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact period of time. I can't pinpoint it. But as far as I know, before I left for Krajina, the air strikes started from their air space, but I would not be able to give you the immediate cause, whether it was taking UNPROFOR members as hostages or something else. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just see if I can orient you just a little bit on this, General. And I'm going to just save some time and read from 65 ter 528. We don't need to put it up on e-court, and this is at page 46, paragraph 189: "The United Nations special representative authorised air strikes at 1620 hours local time on 25 May. At 1633 hours, a NATO liaison officer informed the special representative that six NATO aircraft had attacked two ammunition bunkers in the vicinity of Pale." Let me just stop there, General. Do you remember the ammunition bunkers in Pale being hit? Does that refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the ammunition bunkers were ever targeted; however, I seem to remember that some facilities in Pale were targeted as well as on some signals and communication facilities on Mount Jahorina. That's as much as I can remember. I don't know whether these facilities were targeted during that particular attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This passage continues for just a couple of sentences: "The Serbs again failed to comply, continuing to bombard Sarajevo. They also began retaliating against the safe areas and, in particular, against vulnerable civilian targets in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Tuzla, an air burst weapon exploded in a crowded downtown area killing 71 people, most of them young men and women and injuring almost 200 others." Do you remember this occasion when the safe areas were shelled by the VRS and in particular this incident where over 70 people in Tuzla were killed on May 25, 1995? Do you remember that, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I only heard about this later. I learned about this from the media. And then, by the end of the war, I heard that some officers had been taken to task or indictments were issued for this particular case. However, at the time in the Main Staff we did not receive any reports about these particular actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, General, the Trial Chamber has heard or seen the order from General Milovanovic to take the peacekeepers hostage and deploy them to these various military facilities basic as human targets and we've also heard some testimony about that. So I put it to you that this, the hostage taking was obviously coordinated by the Main Staff, so my question to you is -- and the Trial Chamber has also heard testimony about shelling of Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica, on the same day that the other safe areas were shelled. My question to you is: How was that shelling that day coordinated? I take it that these subordinate commands didn't coincidentally begin shelling all at the same time and that there must have been some coordination involved. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you know about the coordination of that shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General Masal. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Compound, in our submission, in particular, "I put it to you that this hostage taking was obviously coordinated by the Main Staff ..." He should have asked that, putting it, it requires an answer. And then he goes on and asks another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can break down the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can split it up Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My first question, General, is it's the Prosecution's position, based on, for example, the order from General Milovanovic structuring the various corps to take UNPROFOR hostages and deploy them to military facilities, that that was coordinated by the Main Staff. What do you have to say to that proposition, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "coordination" assumes an operation on a large scale. Obviously if the order came from General Milovanovic, and I wasn't there and I don't know who was there, but it is obvious that he must have called the commander and told him what to do. There was no other coordination from one place. There wasn't any from the ops room, or maybe I wasn't there, I don't know. It seems that this was individual order issuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that General Milovanovic served as a witness here, at no point in time did any questions of these -- of this type been put to him, and if the Prosecution had any interest in raising these questions, he should have done so then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We support that submission wholeheartedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't see any reason not to allow this question as long as it's relevant, but we'll see how the witness can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, let me see if I can help by showing the witness a couple of documents, and we'll move through this line of questioning. May we see P2669 A, please. That's going to be the English. Let's make it easier, 2669 B, please. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, take a moment and read this order. I don't know if you've been shown this during your proofing or not. Just let us know when it's okay to scroll up so you can read the rest of the first page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There should be, Mr. President, with this version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got it, Your Honour. I think it's B. That's what it requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So 2669 A is the translation -- or has the translation, I should add.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, I very unhelpfully said B. It's A, as Mr. Thayer has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Are you ready to go down to the bottom of the page, General? Just let us know if you're ready for the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- second page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have the second page in English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, what you've just read indicates that we have four corps that are being involved here pursuant to this order from General Milovanovic to distribute these hostages and put them at warehouses, firing positions, and other potential targets. And the Trial Chamber is seeing a follow-on order from the Drina Corps with respect to this order from General Milovanovic and has heard testimony about the hostages themselves when they were released finally in June. So my question again to you, General, is based on, for example, just seeing this document itself, which indicates the dispersal of these hostages across four corps and the need to keep track of them, make sure that they are secured to these potential targets, again I put it to you that clearly the Main Staff was coordinating this hostage taking and deployment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, General. Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has already answered that question. Mentioning also the Main Staff in this context is unacceptable insofar as it would refer to a collective responsibility and this is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We think that the witness can answer the question. Let's see whether he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never seen this order before, but I repeat what I've already said. This was not coordination. This was an individual act, an order by the deputy corps commander. To what extent this was implemented, I don't know, I wouldn't be able to tell you because I simply don't know. I believe that very few persons -- or maybe just the commander and the Chief of Staff actually were aware of this order and the fact that this order was sent to the corps. It says, after all, that the president of the republic and the entire general public were informed about this, because excerpts from this order were given to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let me just make sure I understand your testimony correctly, General, it's your testimony that based on your knowledge and your experience, there was no Main Staff involvement whatsoever during this hostage taking and deployment to various military installations other than the Chief of Staff and the commander of the Main Staff; is that your testimony? That all this was done with no involvement in the Main Staff other than those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The commander was informed. Otherwise /General Milovanovic would not have sent it. However, I am sure that while I was there the staff was not gathered to either be informed about this order or to be conveyed this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we still have a couple of minutes, but I have another series of questions and I think it would be more fruitful if we broke for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn for today. And General Masal, we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. So as you were told yesterday -- last week, you are not supposed to talk about your evidence with anybody. Tomorrow 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1.43 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of December, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
